newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP congress votes for poll on conscription.
newsitem.headline: German FDP congress votes for poll on conscription.

text.p: A congress of the German Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners, voted on Sunday to poll party members before the next general election on the future of conscription.
A majority at the congress in the spa town of Wiesbaden rejected the party leadership's suggestion to hold the survey in 1999 -- the year after the next general election is due.
FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle warned delegates it could be damaging to the party's election campaign if it appeared divided over the issue of compulsory military service.

But former economics minister Juergen Moellemann said delaying the poll until 1999 would mean the FDP's position could not be included in any new coalition agreement between the party and Kohl's Christian Democrats if they won the election.
This would mean the issue could not be decided in the next parliament, Moellemann said.
German law requires men to serve 10 months in the military but also allows an alternative for objectors of 13 months doing civilian work for hospitals or other good causes.
Many of Bonn's military allies such as France and the Netherlands have recently given national service its marching orders but German politicians have been more wary.
Many see the draft as a guarantee that the military retains a close link to civilian society, avoiding the danger of a "state within a state" or a return to Nazi-style militarism.
